title: Who we are
html: We’re Alyona and Andrei. In the summer of 2018, we cycled across Europe. The trip took 44 days, 24 of them in the saddle. We rode in two stages, from Kaliningrad to Amsterdam and from Copenhagen to Stockholm, covering over 2,000 km by bike in all. Here’s our story, with the route, photos and notes from the road.

title: Getting ready
html:
We first dreamed of a cycling trip after an earlier long trip to Europe. At first we wanted to volunteer through Workaway again, this time bringing our bikes to get from one project to the next. We had less time on this trip and took ages to make up our minds, so we had to drop the idea of volunteering. We decided to set off towards Berlin and see how far we got before the money or the visas ran out.

We did no special training and only rode our bikes now and then before we left.

We had little idea how to pack for a long cycling trip. Skjegg’s blog helped us find bike gear on a budget. He’d written a detailed roundup of local gear makers.

A few other sites and articles helped us get ready.

  • Bikepacking.com covers everything bikepacking.
  • Bicycle Touring Pro has a packing list for a “classic” bike tour.
  • The Adventure Junkies has another packing list. It helps to read a few and compare them.
  • Tom’s Bike Trip has a detailed personal kit list with links.
  • Adventure Cycling Association has tips on saving money on the road.

We got everything together in a hurry. It took us two weeks to read up on bike touring, choose, order and fit the gear, and get the bikes checked over.

title: What we ended up with
html:
Bikes Verenti Substance / Kona Rove
Saddle bags Kravets / Uraltour
Handlebar bags and feed bags Malpa
Front racks Bazhov
Rack bags RackBag
Waist packs Zulu / Graphit

We got the tent, sleeping mats and almost all the rest of our camping gear at Decathlon.

Full packing list

  • Tools. Hex keys, tyre levers, Bike Hand tool, patches, pump, universal bike spanner, dry chain lube, chain breaker, spare bolts, gloves, multitool.
  • Parts and spares. Inner tubes ×2, lights and batteries, bike lock, chain, cable, electrical tape, spare spokes, zip ties, carabiners.
  • Bags and packing. Front bags, handlebar bag, saddle bag, feed bags, waist packs, tool pouch, rack dry bag, rack bungee cords, bottles, bags to pack the bikes for the train.
  • Gear. Reflective vests, rain jacket, sleeping bag, tent, sleeping mat, foil blanket, stove, cooking pot, mugs, spoons, head torch, plastic bags, lighter and matches, thread and needles, side-release buckles, locks, knife, gloves, helmet.
  • Clothes. Sunglasses, T-shirts ×2, jerseys ×2, joggers, jeans, shorts ×2 plus a quick-drying pair, socks and underwear ×4, jumper, beanie, Buff, sandals, towel, notebook and pen, glasses case, string shopping bag.
  • Electronics. Laptop and charger, phones and cables, flash drives, two USB adapters, power bank and cable, headphones, three-way socket splitter, camera with charger and batteries.
  • Documents. Passports (internal and international), international driving permits, medical insurance policies, train tickets, bank card statements.
  • Toiletries. Sunscreen, toothbrush, toothpaste, Dettol, wet wipes, tissues.
  • First aid kit. Activated charcoal, anti-inflammatory medicine, bandages, elastic bandage, plasters, hydrogen peroxide / brilliant green antiseptic / iodine, vitamins.

To take the bikes on the train, we took them apart and packed them in tyre storage bags (ordinary bin bags with a wide opening) and cling film. We took off the front wheel, handlebars, pedals and rack, then wrapped them against the frame. We put cardboard between the parts to keep them from scratching. As we approached the train with all this, the attendants started giving us a hard time, asking questions and saying they wouldn’t let us on with that luggage. You can safely ignore all that and get on. Packed this way, a bike is allowed in an open-plan sleeper carriage. It says so in the carriage rules. The bike itself fits on the top luggage shelf.

title: Kaliningrad
html:
This is how the bikes arrived in Kaliningrad. Two hours later we had them back together and went out to see the city.

We wanted to start fresh, so we spent the night in a hostel and set off the next morning. We just wandered around for the rest of the day and found the tastiest handmade tofu at Plokhoy Okhotnik.

title: Frombork, Poland
html:
We were really nervous about crossing the border by bike, so we loaded up on everything we’d read about on cycling sites. Front and rear lights, reflectors, bells. We put on reflective vests and helmets. In the end, nobody checked any of it. They just asked each of us to open any one of our bags and barely looked inside. The border guards checked our papers, stamped them and waved us through.

Frombork was the first Polish town we stopped in. It has a big castle, Copernicus’s grave and a little port of its own.

title: Malbork
html: The rain forced us to stop. We spent the whole day at Marienburg Castle, an impressive pile of red brick spread over 20 hectares. The history of this castle deserves a story of its own. Start with Wikipedia.

title: Wałcz
html:
Three days on the road and we were stuck again. The rain came down too hard for too long to keep going. We spent two days sheltering from the downpour in a hostel by a lake where Olympic kayakers train. As far as we could tell, a lot of people in Poland love the sport. We stayed at a few campsites set up for kayakers and they were always busy. People go out in big groups, as families, with kids, any way you can think of.

The best thing in Polish cooking is pierogi, otherwise known to us as vareniki. They serve them everywhere, they’re cheap and they’ll keep you going for at least half a day.

title: Germany
html: Our first stop in Germany came as a shock. We found a place to sleep in a camping village where several thousand people lived in vans, motorhomes and tents. Turns out it’s a pretty popular way to live in Germany. You can even register a motorhome as your address and get mail there.

title: Berlin
html: We stayed with a friend for three days. It was our second time here and we still want to go back. It’s such a lively city. If you’re into street art, both the city and the Urban Nation museum are a must.

title: Magdeburg and Hanover
html:
It got really hot. After three days off the road, getting out of Berlin was a bit of a struggle. Our route latched onto the Mittelland Canal and we followed it most of the way to the Netherlands.

On the very first day, Alyona got heatstroke. It’s not terribly dangerous, but it’s pretty unpleasant. Cover your head and use sunscreen. And if it gets you, duck into the shade and sleep for several hours straight. Ten-minute breaks won’t do it.

Along the canal we came across the Magdeburg Water Bridge, a rare and unusual structure. It’s very strange watching big barges float across a bridge with another river down below.

There was always something moving on the canal. To keep ourselves entertained, we started chasing boats, like the railfans in The Station Agent, only on the water. We saw all sorts of boats, from commercial and construction barges to pleasure boats and yachts. People even bring their own cars along on canal trips. Almost everyone on the boats had dogs and bikes.

One of our campsites was right on the canal. The owner turned out to be a Russian German. He invited us into his motorhome, put on Russia’s Channel One and told us a few stories about resettlement, the Russian mafia in Germany and how those camping villages we’d been marvelling at the whole way came to be. Of course, in the morning we watched Live Healthy.

We got caught in the rain in Germany, too. One of those days we were having lunch by a lake with a fortress. The owner invited us inside to wait it out for a couple of hours. He gave us some Coke and showed us around. Turns out it was a real castle with a ghost. The owner showed us the hall where a woman was killed many years ago and the spot on the floor where her body lay. Now her ghost prowls the tower at night and makes terrifying noises. This guy is restoring the castle. His wife and kids were behind the idea at first. After running into the ghost they stopped coming, but the guy got used to it.

title: The Netherlands
html: Campsites in the Netherlands cost twice as much as they did in Germany. So we decided to make a push for Amsterdam without another overnight stop. We had to ride 143 km in a day, but old friends and almost two weeks of rest were waiting for us in the city.

title: Amsterdam
html:
It was our first time here, though we’d planned to come many times. The city brings together a few of our favourite things in one place. Boats, water and bikes. One morning we made a point of getting up early to ride along all the canals in the centre before the tourists came out.

We arrived during Pride, one of Europe’s biggest LGBT festivals. From Friday evening through the whole weekend, the canals filled up with carnival boats and the people on them never stopped partying. There was a parade on one of the main canals, and even the firefighters and police take part every year. The streets were even more packed than the canals. In the centre we just squeezed through the crowd.

In the second half of our “holiday” in Amsterdam we helped the local squatters put on a festival. It had been a while since I’d been part of something so self-organised. It was lovely to see so many different people brought together by a common cause. We met a bunch of interesting people and miss them all a lot.

title: Copenhagen, Denmark
html:
We got to Copenhagen on FlixBus coaches. Some have a special bike rack, so you don’t have to take your bike apart. Still, we’d only use this company as a last resort. We had a connection in Bremen, but the next bus simply didn’t show up. We had to figure out how to get the rest of the way. It all worked out, but we still haven’t got any money back for the tickets, even after a dozen emails to customer support.

We didn’t get to see Copenhagen. Our visas were about to run out, so after a night at a campsite we headed straight for Sweden.

title: Sweden
html:
Wild camping is allowed in Sweden. Better still, there are so many beautiful, deserted places to pitch a tent. We barely stayed at campsites, spending the nights by some lake or behind a rock.

There are fewer cycle paths here, but the roads are quiet and easy to ride on. There were more climbs, but we got used to them quickly. We spent whole days just taking in the scenery. Of the whole trip, we liked the Swedish countryside best.

title: Jönköping
html: We rode about 70 km along the shore of the enormous Lake Vättern. We were watching boats again, but different ones this time. In place of the cargo barges from the German canal, there were lovely yachts, sailboats and pleasure boats. The traditional red-and-white houses were all along the shore. Almost every body of water seems to have one.

title: Norrköping
html:
Here the water opens onto the Baltic Sea and you can smell the salt. We were nearly in Stockholm, so we took more photos and more breaks.
We spotted deer several times while looking for somewhere to camp. On our last night of wild camping, we even pitched our tent in a nature reserve. I’ll definitely remember my 27th birthday. I woke up by a lake in the woods, had breakfast on a warm rock and rode to Stockholm.

title: Stockholm
html: Once again we had no time to see the city. We just rode through the centre, bought a souvenir for some friends and got on the ferry. That was the end of the bike adventure. We made it home the rest of the way by ferry, bus and car. We’d love to go back to the cities we didn’t get to see.

title: How it ended
html:
More happened in those 44 days than we’ve written about here. There were also a nudist campsite, dead opossums on the road and lunch with ticks. We like remembering these stories and telling them. We wanted to give you a taste of our trip and show what this kind of travel can be like. If you’re curious about the details, drop me a line at tarasov.a.dev@gmail.com.

There are more photos of roads, fields and wind turbines in the album on Google Photos.

Thank you
